patterns.usage_note: Concedes something the speaker accepts as fact, then reports that what you would expect from it did not follow; the second clause is usually a shortfall, a doubt, or an unrealized result rather than a neutral contrast. It is more written and more deliberate than けれど or が: unlike にしろ, which concedes a case that may be merely supposed, and たところで, which supposes a futile action, ものの concedes a fact the speaker accepts as true. It also follows a な-adjective + な (便利[べんり]なものの) and a noun + である (事実[じじつ]であるものの).

examples.ruby: 頭[あたま]では分[わ]かっているものの、なかなか実行[じっこう]できない。
examples.english: I understand it well enough in my head, but I just can't put it into practice.

examples.ruby: 値段[ねだん]は高[たか]いものの、品質[ひんしつ]には文句[もんく]のつけようがない。
examples.english: It is expensive, but you can't fault the quality.

examples.ruby: 弟[おとうと]はよく食[た]べるものの、少[すこ]しも太[ふと]らない。
examples.english: My little brother eats plenty, yet he never puts on any weight.

patterns.usage_note: Reports that reality turned out to contradict what the speaker had assumed, so it carries audible surprise; the classical 思ひきや behind it gives it a slightly bookish, storytelling flavor even in casual speech. The base form is と思いきや; か may be added after a noun or question-like clause (かと思いきや), and the outcome is normally something already observed rather than a prediction. Compare ものの, which concedes a fact without any element of surprise.

examples.ruby: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るかと思[おも]いきや、空[そら]はすっかり晴[は]れ上[あ]がった。
examples.english: I was sure it would rain, and instead the sky cleared up completely.

examples.ruby: 簡単[かんたん]な問題[もんだい]かと思[おも]いきや、全然[ぜんぜん]解[と]き方[かた]が分[わ]からない。
examples.english: It looked like an easy problem, but I can't figure out how to solve it at all.

examples.ruby: もう帰[かえ]ったかと思[おも]いきや、まだ会議室[かいぎしつ]に残[のこ]っていた。
examples.english: I assumed he'd gone home, but there he still was in the meeting room.
